# GA-readiness assessment for Llama Stack

## Description

This epic resolves the strategy's central unknown: the full inventory of gaps
between current Llama Stack Tech Preview quality and the GA bar. It produces
the definitive GA scope that all downstream GA work is planned against. The
assessment consolidates scattered TP feedback (support tickets, known issues)
and systematically evaluates the four gap dimensions named by the strategy:
API stability, upgrade paths, scale limits, and error handling.

## Scope

- Consolidate and triage TP feedback from support tickets and other feedback
  channels into a single deduplicated inventory.
- Audit the published API surface (OpenAI-compatible REST APIs and the
  LlamaStackDistribution CRD) for stability gaps: unversioned or
  churn-prone endpoints, undocumented behaviors, breaking changes across
  recent TP releases.
- Assess upgrade paths: what is required to upgrade from the last two TP
  releases, including whether upgrade-test infrastructure exists.
- Assess scale limits: current known ceilings (concurrent distributions,
  request throughput, resource footprint) versus GA expectations.
- Assess error handling: failure modes, error surfaced to users, retry and
  degradation behavior.
- For each gap, classify it as must-fix-for-GA vs. deferrable, and map it to
  the owning workstream (API stability hardening, support posture, TrustyAI
  guardrails integration, Dashboard enablement).
- Produce a GA scope document defining the definitive GA scope, and obtain
  stakeholder acceptance of it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A GA-readiness gap inventory exists covering all four named dimensions
  (API stability, upgrade paths, scale limits, error handling), with every
  gap classified as must-fix-for-GA or deferrable and mapped to an owning
  workstream.
- TP feedback from support tickets is triaged and reflected in the inventory
  (no known TP feedback channel left unconsolidated).
- A GA scope document is produced and accepted by the strategy's
  stakeholders, defining what is in and out of GA scope.
- The assessment explicitly states whether upgrade-test infrastructure for
  the last two TP releases exists, and what is needed if not.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): GA-readiness assessment inventories the gaps between current
  TP quality and GA bar, producing the definitive GA scope — this epic is
  the direct delivery of HLR-1.

## Notes

- This investigation gates all implementation workstreams in this strategy
  (API stability, support posture, guardrails integration, Dashboard
  enablement): the strategy's Open Question 1 states the size of the
  stability and hardening work is an estimate until this assessment lands.
  Downstream epics carry a rewrite gate against it.
- The outcome space is an unbounded gap inventory (not a small bounded set
  of alternatives), so downstream work is gated and phased rather than
  split into conditional branch epics.

# Llama Stack API stability guarantees and tested upgrade path

## Description

This epic delivers the API stability guarantee for the published Llama Stack
surface required for GA: versioned APIs, a deprecation policy, and a tested
upgrade path from the last two TP releases. It hardens the Tech Preview API
surface (OpenAI-compatible REST APIs and the LlamaStackDistribution CRD) to
the point where a stability commitment can be published and honored.

## Scope

- Introduce API versioning across the published Llama Stack API surface
  (REST APIs and the LlamaStackDistribution CRD), following the versioning
  approach resolved during implementation.
- Define the deprecation policy as normative engineering policy: how API
  changes are versioned, how deprecations are announced, and how long
  deprecated surfaces remain supported.
- Remediate API-stability gaps classified as must-fix-for-GA by the
  GA-readiness assessment.
- Build and execute upgrade-path tests from the last two TP releases to the
  GA release (including whatever upgrade-test infrastructure proves
  necessary), producing repeatable evidence.
- Record the stability guarantee statement for the GA API surface as a
  normative engineering commitment, delivered as input to the GA
  documentation workstream for user-facing authoring.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The published API surface is versioned, and the versioning scheme is
  documented.
- A deprecation policy is defined as normative policy content and
  consistently applied: any TP API surface not carried into GA is either
  preserved per policy or explicitly deprecated with a migration path.
- A tested upgrade path from each of the last two TP releases to the GA
  release exists, with repeatable test evidence (automated where feasible).
- All API-stability gaps classified as must-fix-for-GA by the GA-readiness
  assessment are remediated or explicitly deferred with stakeholder
  sign-off recorded in the assessment's scope document.
- The stability guarantee statement is recorded as a normative engineering
  commitment alongside the GA API surface, as input to the GA
  documentation workstream (user-facing authoring happens there).

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (P0): Published API surface carries a stability guarantee —
  versioned APIs, deprecation policy, and a tested upgrade path from the
  last two TP releases. This epic is the direct delivery of HLR-2.

## Notes

- Scope is gated by the GA-readiness assessment: the definitive set of
  must-fix stability gaps (and the state of upgrade-test infrastructure)
  is determined by that assessment; if it finds the hardening work larger
  or smaller than estimated, this epic's scope is rewritten accordingly.
- Documentation boundary: this epic delivers normative engineering policy
  (the versioning scheme, deprecation policy, and stability guarantee
  commitment) only. The user-facing documentation set — including the
  API reference and deprecation-policy documentation — is authored by
  the GA documentation workstream from this epic's normative output.

# Llama Stack production support posture

## Description

This epic establishes the production support posture required for Llama
Stack GA: documented SLO targets, a backport policy, and a supported
configuration matrix. It converts the Tech Preview "best effort" posture
into defined, supportable commitments.

## Scope

- Define SLO targets for the Llama Stack distribution as normative policy
  content (availability and responsiveness objectives appropriate to a GA
  supported component, validated against realistic configurations where
  feasible).
- Define the backport policy as normative policy content: which release
  trains receive fixes, for how long, and how security and critical fixes
  are delivered.
- Define and document the supported configuration matrix: the provider
  combinations (e.g., inference and vector providers), deployment sizes,
  and platform versions that are supported at GA, aligned with the
  GA-readiness assessment's findings.
- Remediate support-posture gaps classified as must-fix-for-GA by the
  GA-readiness assessment.
- Deliver the support posture (SLO targets, backport policy, supported
  configuration matrix) as normative policy content for the GA
  documentation workstream, which authors the user-facing support
  documentation where support and customers consume it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- SLO targets are defined as normative policy content for the GA
  distribution, with the measurement approach stated for each target.
- The backport policy is documented, covering fix scope, supported release
  trains, and duration.
- The supported configuration matrix is documented, and every entry is
  either validated or explicitly marked experimental/unsupported.
- All support-posture gaps classified as must-fix-for-GA by the
  GA-readiness assessment are remediated or explicitly deferred with
  stakeholder sign-off recorded in the assessment's scope document.
- The normative support posture content is reviewed and accepted by the
  stakeholders who own support commitments; the user-facing support
  documentation is authored by the GA documentation workstream.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P0): Production support posture is in place — documented SLO
  targets, backport policy, and supported configuration matrix. This epic
  is the direct delivery of HLR-3.

## Notes

- Scope is gated by the GA-readiness assessment: the supported
  configuration matrix and any hardening required to meet SLO targets
  follow from the assessment's gap inventory; if it changes the GA scope,
  this epic's scope is rewritten accordingly.
- SLO and backport commitments require human approval (support/product
  sign-off) as an explicit part of the deliverable.
- Documentation boundary: this epic defines the support posture as
  normative policy content only. The user-facing support-posture
  documentation is authored by the GA documentation workstream from this
  epic's normative output.

# Supported TrustyAI guardrails integration in Llama Stack GA distributions

## Description

This epic promotes the TrustyAI safety-guardrails integration in Llama Stack
from an experimental flag to a supported, documented integration in GA
distributions. After this epic, users of GA Llama Stack distributions can
configure TrustyAI-backed safety guardrails as a supported capability with
documentation and defined behavior, not an opt-in experiment.

## Scope

- Promote the TrustyAI guardrails integration from experimental flag to a
  supported configuration in Llama Stack GA distributions, following the
  promotion mechanism resolved during implementation.
- Remediate guardrails-integration gaps classified as must-fix-for-GA by
  the GA-readiness assessment (the strategy's problem statement
  specifically calls out quality gaps that TP status excuses).
- Define the supported integration surface: which TrustyAI guardrail
  capabilities are supported through the Llama Stack safety provider
  interface, its configuration mechanism, and its limitations, recorded
  as normative engineering input for the GA documentation workstream
  (the user-facing guardrails documentation is authored there, not in
  this epic).
- Coordinate with the TrustyAI team's end-to-end validation of the
  integration and resolve or document issues it surfaces.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A GA Llama Stack distribution can be configured with TrustyAI safety
  guardrails without any experimental or TP opt-in flag.
- The supported integration surface is defined and recorded as normative
  engineering input — configuration mechanism, supported capabilities,
  and known limitations — for the GA documentation workstream that
  authors the user-facing documentation.
- All guardrails-integration gaps classified as must-fix-for-GA by the
  GA-readiness assessment are remediated or explicitly deferred with
  stakeholder sign-off recorded in the assessment's scope document.
- Functional testing of the guardrails integration passes against a
  TrustyAI service instance in a GA-distribution configuration.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-4 (P1): Safety guardrails via TrustyAI are a supported, documented
  integration (not an experimental flag) for GA distributions. This epic
  is the primary delivery of HLR-4 on the Llama Stack distribution side;
  the TrustyAI-side validation of the same integration is tracked
  separately by the TrustyAI team.

## Notes

- Scope is gated by the GA-readiness assessment: whether the integration
  can be promoted as-is or needs GA-bar remediation is an assessment
  outcome; if the assessment finds the gap larger than estimated, this
  epic's scope is rewritten accordingly.
- This epic's work spans two strategy components (Llama Stack, where the
  integration is wired and supported, and TrustyAI, the guardrails
  backend). Llama Stack is the most-relevant canonical component because
  the change — removing the experimental flag and supporting the
  integration — lands in the distribution.
- Documentation boundary: this epic delivers only the distribution-side
  promotion, remediation, and the normative definition of the supported
  integration surface. All user-facing guardrails documentation
  (configuration steps, supported capabilities, limitations) is authored
  by the GA documentation workstream, which consumes this epic's
  normative output as input.

# TrustyAI-side validation of the guardrails integration with Llama Stack

## Description

This epic delivers the TrustyAI team's validation that TrustyAI guardrails
work as a supported backend for Llama Stack GA distributions. The TrustyAI
service is already GA; its role in this strategy is verification —
confirming that TrustyAIService instances function correctly as the safety
provider for Llama Stack distributions promoted out of experimental status,
and surfacing any TrustyAI-side gaps or incompatibilities.

## Scope

- Define and execute an end-to-end validation plan for TrustyAI guardrails
  as the safety provider in Llama Stack GA distribution configurations,
  covering the scenarios in the supported configuration matrix relevant to
  the integration.
- Validate the TrustyAI-side integration points the Llama Stack safety
  provider relies on (service provisioning per data science project,
  guardrail API behavior, failure and error propagation).
- Record validation evidence: pass/fail per scenario, reproductions for any
  failure, and an assessment of whether each failure is a TrustyAI-side
  defect, a distribution-side defect, or a documentation gap.
- Surface discovered TrustyAI-side gaps with severity classification, and
  either resolve in-scope (if must-fix-for-GA per the GA-readiness
  assessment) or document as known limitations.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A validation plan exists covering the integration scenarios relevant to
  the supported configuration matrix, with defined pass/fail criteria per
  scenario.
- End-to-end validation is executed against the supported Llama Stack
  distribution integration, and a validation evidence report is produced.
- Every failure found is triaged (TrustyAI-side defect, distribution-side
  defect, or documentation gap), with must-fix-for-GA items resolved or
  explicitly deferred with stakeholder sign-off.
- The TrustyAI team confirms (or qualifies, with documented limitations)
  that TrustyAI guardrails are supported as a backend for Llama Stack GA
  distributions.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-4 (P1): Safety guardrails via TrustyAI are a supported, documented
  integration for GA distributions. This epic delivers the TrustyAI-team
  validation half of HLR-4; the distribution-side integration work is
  tracked separately by the RHOAI GenAI team.

## Notes

- This epic is the passive-component exception applied to TrustyAI: the
  strategy lists TrustyAI as affected, and because a different team
  (TrustyAI) validates that component, the validation is a separate
  Implementation epic owned by that team rather than an acceptance
  criterion on the distribution-side epic.
- Scope is gated by the GA-readiness assessment, and the validation runs
  against the delivered distribution-side integration, so it is serial
  after both.

The `decompose_complete=true` line must be your **final action** — the pipeline will not launch the review agent until it is set.\n35\t\n36\tIf neither check fires, proceed to Step 1.\n37\t\n38\t## Step 1: Parse Strategy Structure\n39\t\n40\tExtract these sections from the strategy:\n41\t\n42\t- **Affected Components table**: (component name, what changes, owner team)\n43\t- **Impacted Teams table**: (team, components owned, involvement)\n44\t- **High Level Requirements**: with P0/P1/P2 priority\n45\t- **Dependencies table**: (dependency, type, status, impact if blocked)\n46\t- **Acceptance Criteria**: (Given/When/Then with \"measured by\" clauses)\n47\t- **Non-Functional Requirements**\n48\t\n49\tIf any required section is missing, note it as a health warning but proceed with available information.\n50\t\n51\t## Step 1.5: Parse Staff Engineer Input\n52\t\n53\tIf the strategy contains a Staff Engineer Input section that is non-empty (beyond template placeholder text):\n54\t\n55\t- Parse it first — it takes precedence\n56\t- When Staff Engineer Input diverges from AI-generated Technical Approach, use the Staff Engineer Input\n57\t- Log each override for traceability in the decomposition summary\n58\t\n59\t## Step 2: Build Component Graph\n60\t\n61\t**Component name constraint:** Read `.context/rhai-components.txt` for the canonical list of RHAI Jira components. Match the strategy's Affected Components to the closest canonical name; when one epic's work spans several strategy components, assign the single most-relevant canonical name and note the span in the decomposition summary. `submit.py` silently strips any component not in the list, leaving the Jira epic component-less. Log any non-obvious mappings in the decomposition summary.\n62\t\n63\tFor each (component, change, owner team) tuple from the Affected Components table:\n64\t\n65\t**Active vs. Passive classification:**\n66\t- **Active component**: Code changes needed → generates epic(s)\n67\t- **Passive component**: No code changes, keep working → validation becomes acceptance criterion on nearest active component's epic\n68\t- **Exception**: If a different team validates the passive component → generate a separate validation Implementation epic owned by that team\n69\t\n70\t**New component detection:**\n71\t- Check `.context/architecture-context/` for component existence\n72\t- Component is \"in platform\" if an architecture context file exists for it\n73\t- Component NOT in architecture context → create:\n74\t  - Implementation epic(s) for provisioning with appropriate `implementation_type`\n75\t  - Investigation epic if dependency availability needs validation\n76\t\n77\t## Step 3: Identify Investigation Epics\n78\t\n79\tFirst, systematically scan the strategy for all unknowns — check the open questions table, risks table, assumptions, pending reviews, and conditional ADRs. Do not rely on the technical approach section alone; open questions are often in tables at the end of the strategy and may contradict or qualify the detailed technical description.\n80\t\n81\tCollect the full list of unknowns before creating any Investigation epics. Then evaluate each independently:\n82\t\n83\t**Decision rule: Does the answer change which downstream epics exist or what they do?**\n84\t\n85\t- **YES** → Investigation epic. Determine which downstream epics depend on the outcome. Add as DAG edges. For bounded outcomes (≤3 possibilities): output conditional decomposition branches.\n86\t- **NO** → Acceptance criterion on the relevant Implementation epic. Implementation proceeds the same way regardless; failure = fix-and-retry.\n87\t\n88\tMultiple independent unknowns can produce multiple Investigation epics, even for the same component and team. The component/team boundary rule applies to Implementations (bundling work for a team), not Investigations (resolving a specific unknown). However, if two qualifying unknowns would be resolved by the same experiment producing the same deliverable, combine them into one Investigation — don't split for the sake of splitting.\n89\t\n90\t## Step 4: Map HLRs to Epics\n91\t\n92\t**Precondition:** This step only runs for strategies that were NOT triaged in Step 0. If Step 0 produced a below-threshold or docs-only result, the strategy is already a single epic — do not apply priority-split logic.\n93\t\n94\t- Each P0/P1/P2 requirement must map to one or more epics\n95\t- Every HLR must be covered — no orphaned requirements\n96\t- Priority inheritance: prerequisite epic inherits the highest priority of all HLRs it transitively enables\n97\t- An epic blocking all P0 work is implicitly P0\n98\t- Priority split: when an epic maps to HLRs at multiple priority levels, check whether the lower-priority HLRs represent distinct, deferrable features. A feature is \"distinct and deferrable\" only when it could ship as its own epic with independent user value AND does not share data structures, UI surfaces, or API endpoints with the P0 work. If yes, split them into separate epics by priority so each can be planned independently. If the lower-priority HLR is incidental to the P0 work (error handling, doc coverage, config override that falls out of the same implementation) or is tightly coupled to the same implementation surface, keep it bundled — splitting tightly coupled work creates duplication and artificial boundaries.\n99\t- **Redundant / overlapping HLRs — consolidate, never split:** strategies merged from multiple sources sometimes state one capability twice in different words (e.g. \"select two or more runs and view their parameters and metrics side by side\" and \"a diff view highlighting which parameters and metrics changed between two selected runs\" — the diff view is a presentation mode of the same comparison surface over the same run data). When two HLRs describe the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint for the same component and team — one a restatement or presentation mode of the other — they are ONE capability: cover both with a single epic whose HLR Traceability lists both HLR ids, at the higher of the two priorities. Do not split them into separate epics by priority label: on a shared surface a P0/P1 pair is redundant wording, not a deferral signal, and splitting produces two epics building the same surface plus an artificial serialization edge between them — a boundary violation even when the second epic only extends the first's surface.\n100\t- `docs-authoring` priority exception: `docs-authoring` epics are exempt from priority inheritance. They do not push their priority upstream to the implementations they depend on. Instead, derive their priority from the strategy frontmatter `priority` field: Critical→P0, Major→P1, Normal/Minor/Undefined→P2. If the field is missing or empty, default to P2.\n101\t\n102\t## Step 5: Build Dependency DAG\n103\t\n104\tApply these rules to construct edges between epics:\n105\t\n106\t### Epic Boundary Rules\n107\t1. Different component OR different team → separate epics\n108\t2. Same component + same team + same logical change → single epic. When splitting within a single component, split along two axes:\n109\t   - **Architectural sub-system boundaries**: backend API vs. frontend plugin, Go service vs. React UI, etc.\n110\t   - **Work-product type boundaries**: code implementation, content authoring (sample notebooks, tutorials, curated examples), and documentation are different kinds of work — they require different skills, different review criteria, and produce different PR review cycles. A `konflux-onboarding → general` edge serializes work that must run in parallel and is a rule violation.\n124\t11. `docs-authoring` blocked by ALL Implementation epics in strategy (always last; docs describe what was built). These edges do not trigger priority inheritance — see Step 4 `docs-authoring` priority exception.\n125\t\n126\t### Implementation → Implementation Edges\n127\t12. Does NOT apply to configuration references (image digests, endpoint URLs) — those are AC gates. **In particular, an image digest / SHA consumed by OLM/CSV packaging (`RELATED_IMAGE`) is a configuration reference, not a build-against artifact: the packaging epic gets a \"pinned image digest available\" AC, NOT a `dependencies` edge on the image-build or `konflux-onboarding` epic.** Wiring such an edge both mis-serializes parallel work and violates Rule 10 — the digest is filled in at execution time, so the epics run in parallel.\n129\t14. Implementations in same repo, different areas → parallel (merge conflicts = coordination risk, not dependency)\n131\t\n132\t### External Dependency Edges\n133\t16. New component not in architecture context → generate onboarding chain: `repo-onboarding` + `license-validation` (parallel start) → `konflux-onboarding` (after repo-onboarding) → general implementation (after license-validation; parallel with konflux-onboarding). If viable fallback exists (cherry-pick, fork) → note as AC, not separate epic. If third party resolves → model as precondition with tiered delivery, no separate epic.\n141\t22. Strategy replaces existing capability → add rollback/feature-flag AC to replacing Implementation epic\n145\t24. `docs-authoring` epic → add \"technically reviewed against implementation\" AC\n146\t25. Implementation with `konflux-onboarding` in dependency chain → add \"build pipeline green\" AC\n147\t\n148\t## Step 5.5: Detect Tiered Delivery\n149\t\n150\tWhen an external dependency has uncertain timing:\n151\t\n152\t1. Can the strategy deliver partial value without it?\n153\t2. **YES** → Split into:\n154\t   - **Tier 1**: Independent work (user-facing features OR risk-reduction spikes/validations)\n155\t   - **Tier 2**: Dependency-gated work (blocked by upstream epic)\n156\t3. **NO** → Linear dependencies; external dependency blocks all downstream\n157\t\n158\t## Step 6: Classify Epics\n159\t\n160\tFor each epic, determine:\n161\t\n162\t### Type (mandatory)\n163\t- **Implementation**: Produce an artifact (code, config, docs, manifests, pipelines, RFCs, upstream PRs)\n164\t- **Investigation**: Resolve uncertainty (answer a question or make a decision that other epics depend on)\n165\t\n166\t### Implementation Type (optional routing label)\n167\t\n168\t| Label | When to apply |\n169\t|-------|--------------|\n170\t| `docs-authoring` | Red Hat docs content process — specialized tooling |\n171\t| `konflux-onboarding` | Build pipeline onboarding — known-recipe |\n172\t| `license-validation` | License scanning for transitive dependencies |\n173\t| `repo-onboarding` | Midstream repo fork creation under opendatahub-io |\n174\t| _(absent/null)_ | General-purpose — read target repo, figure it out |\n175\t\n176\t### AI Implementability Signals\n177\t\n178\tScore signals so the pipeline can compute an AI-implementability classification deterministically. **Do not compute the total score or classification yourself.** Use the signal set that matches the epic `type` — Implementation and Investigation epics measure different things.\n179\t\n180\t#### Implementation epics → `ai_signals` (9 signals)\n181\t\n182\tEvaluate each as +1 (favorable), 0 (neutral/N/A), or -1 (unfavorable). Write the values into `ai_signals`.\n183\t\n184\t| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | +1 Condition | -1 Condition |\n185\t|---|--------|----------------|-------------|-------------|\n186\t| 1 | Change specificity | `change_specificity` | Exact file paths, API endpoints, field names known | Vague scope (\"improve X\") |\n187\t| 2 | Pattern precedent | `pattern_precedent` | Similar changes exist in same codebase | No precedent in codebase |\n188\t| 3 | Adapter/plugin pattern | `adapter_pattern` | Follows existing reference implementation | N/A (0 if absent) |\n189\t| 4 | Existing foundation | `existing_foundation` | Extending existing code/feature | Greenfield, no foundation |\n190\t| 5 | Open questions | `open_questions` | All design decisions resolved for this epic | Open questions that would change implementation approach |\n191\t| 6 | External dependency | `external_dependency` | None | Upstream contribution or vendor coordination needed |\n192\t| 7 | Human process gates | `human_process_gates` | None | Requires human approval step |\n193\t| 8 | Repo access | `repo_access` | AI can clone and modify target repo | Repo inaccessible or special access required |\n194\t| 9 | Architecture claims | `architecture_claims` | Strategy cites specific architecture context files/APIs | Unsubstantiated architecture claims |\n195\t\n196\t#### Investigation epics → `investigation_signals` (5 signals)\n197\t\n198\t**Do not use the 9 Implementation signals for Investigation epics.** Those penalize the *defining* traits of an investigation (open questions, no prior foundation, external dependency), so they mis-route nearly every investigation to Low — even ones the AI resolves easily. Instead score these five, which predict whether the AI investigation skill can resolve the unknowns (→ assign to the skill) or a person must (→ assign to a person). Write the values into `investigation_signals`.\n199\t\n200\t| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | Range | How to score |\n201\t|---|--------|-----------------|-------|--------------|\n202\t| 1 | Question specificity | `question_specificity` | -1 / 0 / +1 | +1 concrete, enumerable questions with a defined pass/fail criterion; -1 vague or criterion undefined (a human must frame it first) |\n203\t| 2 | Source accessibility | `source_accessibility` | 0 / +1 | +1 a readable artifact that **contains or determines the answer** exists (open repo, docs, public record). 0 when the only readable material does **not** hold the answer — e.g. a decision/PR still under review (the answer doesn't exist yet) |\n204\t| 3 | Local runnability | `local_runnability` | 0 / +1 | +1 the components can be exercised as a downloaded **binary or pip/npm library** locally — including backing a datastore with an embedded/bundled server (e.g. `pgserver` for PostgreSQL). 0 only if it genuinely can't run without a container/cluster |\n205\t| 4 | Cluster/hardware dependence | `cluster_hardware_dependence` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 some *peripheral* questions need a live cluster / GPU / prod-scale. -2 a *gating* question does. **What an operator/controller _generates_** (rendered CR, template, NetworkPolicy, RBAC in its source repo) is readable source — score it under `source_accessibility`, **not** here; only the *as-deployed runtime state* of a live cluster counts as a dependence |\n206\t| 5 | Human judgment required | `human_judgment_required` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 a *peripheral* question needs a stakeholder/product decision or external-party input. -2 the *gating* question is itself a human/governance decision or external coordination the AI cannot make (e.g. \"is this ADR approved?\") |\n207\t\n208\tThe pipeline routes: **High** → assign to the investigation skill; **Medium** → hybrid (skill resolves the desk/local parts and hands a spec to a human for the rest); **Low** → assign to a person.\n209\t\n210\tWrite the signal rationale to a separate file `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN-ai-signals.md` (one per epic), for whichever signal set you used. Format as a markdown table with Signal, Value, and Rationale columns. Do not write the signals table into the epic body.\n211\t\n212\t## Step 6.5: Health Warnings\n213\t\n214\t### Non-blocking warnings (decomposition proceeds, human verifies later)\n215\t- Priority inversions (P0/P1/P2 inconsistent with technical complexity/reliability)\n216\t- Scope traps: ACs implying infrastructure that doesn't exist, contradictions between out-of-scope items and NFRs, storage beyond design intent\n217\t\n218\t### Handling unclear strategy passages\n219\t\n220\tWhen the strategy is unclear about something, apply this two-way distinction:\n221\t\n222\t| Situation | Handling |\n223\t|-----------|---------|\n224\t| **Implementation detail** — the team will resolve this when they start the work (version choices, API surface discovery, config decisions, validation of assumptions) | Not a flag. Capture as an AC on the relevant epic if needed. Most unclear passages fall here. |\n225\t| **Genuine unknown** — nobody knows yet, resolution requires technical work, and the answer changes which downstream epics exist or what they do | Investigation epic with conditional downstream epics. |\n226\t\n227\tWhen a strategy explicitly flags something as an open question, pending review, or conditional ADR, treat it as a genuine unknown — the strategy author has already classified it. Do not downgrade to an implementation detail based on descriptive text elsewhere in the strategy. A detailed description of current state is context, not a decision. If the strategy indicates the resolution could require a different approach (conditional ADRs, \"if X requires changes to Y\"), evaluate which downstream epics build on the current assumption and gate them on the resolution.\n228\t\n229\t## Step 7: Derive Acceptance Criteria\n230\t\n231\tEach epic gets acceptance criteria derived from:\n232\t- Strategy acceptance criteria allocated to this epic's scope\n233\t- HLRs mapped to this epic\n234\t- Implementation-specific requirements (build pipeline green, rollback plan, doc review, etc.)\n235\t- Rules 23-25 from Step 5\n236\t\n237\tEvery AC must be a testable pass/fail condition on THIS epic's own deliverable. External schedule constraints are not ACs: turnaround you do not control (accredited-lab queues, review-board cadence, upstream vendor timing) belongs in the epic's Risks/Notes or the summary's Health Warnings. Write the AC at the engineering completion point you do control — \"the evidence package is submitted to the certification lab and triaged\" is a valid AC; \"lab scheduling and review-board cadence are externally controlled and cannot be compressed\" is a schedule-risk note misfiled as an AC.\n238\t\n239\t## Step 8: Generate Artifacts\n240\t\n241\t### Step 8a: Write decomposition summary (the plan)\n242\t\n243\tWrite the decomposition summary **first** — this is the blueprint for all epic files.\n244\t\n245\tWrite `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md` in two steps:\n246\t\n247\t1. Write the body content (no frontmatter delimiters) with these sections:\n248\t   - **Epic List** (table: ID, title, type, team, priority)\n249\t   - **Dependency DAG** (Mermaid `graph TD` diagram — roots at top, arrows point from dependency to dependent: `E001 --> E003` means \"E001 must complete before E003 can start\")\n250\t   - **DAG Justification** (table: edge, rule, rationale)\n251\t   - **HLR Traceability Matrix** (HLR → epic mapping, confirming full coverage)\n252\t   - **Health Warnings** (priority inversions, scope traps — if any)\n253\t   - **Tiered Delivery** (if applicable — Tier 1 vs Tier 2 split)\n254\t\n255\t2. Set frontmatter via script:\n256\t\n257\t```bash\n258\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md \\\n259\t    parent_strat=\"{ID}\" epic_count=<N> critical_path_length=<N>\n260\t```\n261\t\n262\tAdd `triage=<value> triage_rationale=\"<reason>\"` for triaged strategies (Step 0).\n263\t\n264\t### Scope constraint: decompose, don't design\n265\t\n266\tYour job is to break strategy scope into units of work, not to make implementation decisions.\n267\tIf the strategy describes a capability at a functional level, the epic scope stays at that level.\n268\tDo not invent API paths, URL schemas, response formats, environment variables, caching policies,\n269\tCRD field names, or other implementation details not stated in the strategy. Those are decisions\n270\tfor the implementing team.\n271\t\n272\t### Step 8b: Write per-epic files\n273\t\n274\tWrite one file per epic to `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN.md` (e.g., `{ID}-E001.md`, `{ID}-E002.md`), following the decomposition summary as the plan. Each epic's `dependencies`, `priority`, `type`, and HLR mappings must match what the summary specifies.\n275\t\n276\tFor each epic, write in two steps:\n277\t\n278\t1. Write the body content (no frontmatter delimiters) with these sections (minimum — add additional sections when the strategy contains relevant content for this epic's scope, e.g., risks, assumptions, open questions, stakeholder commitments):\n279\t   - **Title** (one line)\n280\t   - **Description** (what this epic delivers)\n281\t   - **Scope** (specific changes in this epic)\n282\t   - **Acceptance Criteria** (derived from strategy)\n283\t   - **HLR Traceability** (which strategy HLRs this epic covers)\n284\t   The four section headings are literal and required for EVERY epic, including `docs-authoring` epics — an outline of content topics goes INSIDE the `## Scope` section, never as a renamed `## Content Outline` heading (a renamed heading fails the artifact contract).\n285\t   Signal rationales go in a separate file (see Step 6) — do not include them in the epic body.\n286\t\n287\t   **No cross-references to sibling epics.** Do not reference other epics by draft ID (e.g., \"E001\", \"E003\") anywhere in the body — not in descriptions, scope, acceptance criteria, or HLR traceability. Each epic body must be self-contained: describe what it delivers and depends on in plain terms (e.g., \"the OTEL env var injection capability\" not \"E003\") without naming sibling epics.\n288\t\n289\t2. Set frontmatter via script:\n290\t\n291\t```bash\n292\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-E001.md \\\n293\t    epic_id=\"{ID}-E001\" title=\"<epic title>\" parent_strat=\"{ID}\" \\\n294\t    component=\"<canonical name from .context/rhai-components.txt>\" team=\"<owner team>\" \\\n295\t    type=Implementation priority=P0 \\\n296\t    dependencies=\"{ID}-E002,{ID}-E003\" \\\n297\t    ai_signals.change_specificity=1 \\\n298\t    ai_signals.pattern_precedent=1 \\\n299\t    ai_signals.adapter_pattern=0 \\\n300\t    ai_signals.existing_foundation=1 \\\n301\t    ai_signals.open_questions=-1 \\\n302\t    ai_signals.external_dependency=0 \\\n303\t    ai_signals.human_process_gates=-1 \\\n304\t    ai_signals.repo_access=1 \\\n305\t    ai_signals.architecture_claims=1\n306\t```\n307\t\n308\tFor an **Investigation** epic, set `type=Investigation` and write the five\n309\t`investigation_signals` instead of `ai_signals` (do not set both):\n310\t\n311\t```bash\n312\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-E001.md \\\n313\t    epic_id=\"{ID}-E001\" title=\"<epic title>\" parent_strat=\"{ID}\" \\\n314\t    component=\"<canonical name>\" team=\"<owner team>\" \\\n315\t    type=Investigation priority=P0 \\\n316\t    investigation_signals.question_specificity=1 \\\n317\t    investigation_signals.source_accessibility=1 \\\n318\t    investigation_signals.local_runnability=1 \\\n319\t    investigation_signals.cluster_hardware_dependence=0 \\\n320\t    investigation_signals.human_judgment_required=0\n321\t```\n322\t\n323\tAdd optional fields only when non-null: `implementation_type=<value>`, `branch=<value>`, `gated_by=<epic_id>`, `gate_failure_impact.action=<value> gate_failure_impact.fallback_approach=\"<text>\"`. Every epic that depends on an Investigation should have `gated_by` pointing to that Investigation (see Rule 3).\n324\t\n325\tDo **not** include `ai_implementability` or `ai_implementability_score` — the pipeline computes those from `ai_signals` (Implementation) or `investigation_signals` (Investigation) automatically.\n326\t\n327\t### Step 8c: Verify consistency\n328\t\n329\tAfter writing all epic files, run:\n330\t```\n331\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py batch-read artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-*E[0-9][0-9][0-9].md\n332\t```\n333\t\n334\tCompare the output against the decomposition summary.
